question: Identify candidate fusion gene junctions from RNA-Seq data. Align reads with STAR using chimeric detection parameters to produce a chimeric junction file, then extract candidate fusion junctions into a CSV.

files.eval_guideline: Junction records must match the reference in donor and acceptor chromosome, position, and strand; read-level annotation columns may differ.
files.match_reasoning: Identical filename; both are STAR chimeric junction files (.junction).

parameters.question: Compare STAR Chimeric.out.junction records for candidate fusion junctions. Rows must match on donor chromosome, donor position, donor strand, acceptor chromosome, acceptor position, and acceptor strand (columns 1-6). Read-level annotation columns (junction type, repeat lengths, read name, alignment starts, CIGARs, etc.) may differ and should be ignored. Row order may differ.

files.strategy_reasoning: STAR chimeric alignment is deterministic, and the guideline asks for a record-by-record match on donor and acceptor chromosome, position and strand, while allowing the read-level annotation columns to differ. Approximate comparison fits this because it lines up rows and columns flexibly and can ignore the columns that don't matter.

align_plan.reasoning: The reference has no header and uses the first 14 columns of STAR's Chimeric.out.junction format. The candidate has the same 14 columns with names, then 7 extra columns from newer STAR versions (multimapping chimera scores, PEmerged, readgrp). The values in the preview line up position by position, so ref columns 0–13 map to the first 14 candidate columns in order. No transpose is needed. I used the junction coordinates (donor and acceptor chromosome, breakpoint and strand, ref columns 0–5) as the key, as the evaluation guideline requires. I added read_name (column 9), which comes straight from the input reads, because coordinates alone repeat across reads that support the same junction. The candidate has extra rows (757 vs 434), mostly from multimapping chimeric alignments, so rows are matched by key rather than by position. The output is an unordered set of junction records, so row order doesn't matter. The read-level annotation columns (alignment starts, CIGAR strings, junction type, repeat lengths) can legitimately differ and are mapped but not used as keys.

column_configs.reasoning: Junction type annotation (-1/0/1/2). It is an annotation, not part of the junction coordinates, and depends on STAR version and settings. The guideline allows it to differ.
Repeat length to the left of the junction. This is an annotation the guideline allows to differ.
Repeat length to the right of the junction. This is an annotation the guideline allows to differ.
First base of the donor segment for each read. This is read-level alignment detail, not junction identity.
Donor CIGAR string. It is read-level and depends on how soft-clipping and alignment were done.
First base of the acceptor segment for each read. This is read-level alignment detail.
Acceptor CIGAR string. It is read-level and differs between runs (for example, 73M3S vs 71M86N5M).

comparison_plan.overall_reasoning:
The evaluation guideline says a junction record matches when its donor and acceptor chromosome, position and strand match the reference. Those fields are columns 0–5, and they are already used as ID columns to align the rows, along with read name (column 9). Whether a junction is found therefore depends on row alignment, not on comparing values.

The other columns are all read-level annotations from STAR's Chimeric.out.junction file:
- column 6: junction type
- columns 7 and 8: repeat lengths to the left and right of the junction
- column 10: first base of the donor segment
- column 11: donor CIGAR
- column 12: first base of the acceptor segment
- column 13: acceptor CIGAR

The guideline says these may differ. They also do differ between STAR versions and parameter settings:
- Mate CIGARs can be clipped differently (for example, 14293p71M86N5M vs 14293p73M3S).
- Junction type and repeat values can change.
- The extra columns in the candidate output (num_chim_aln, scores, readgrp) do not exist in the reference.

So every non-ID column is set to 'ignore', and scoring rests on whether the ID columns match during alignment.

notes: Scored by overlap of row keys (F1)

parameters.question: Compare candidate fusion junction tables from STAR chimeric detection. Fusion records must match the reference in chr1, base1, strand1, chr2, base2, strand2, and junction_type; row and column order may differ.

files.strategy_reasoning: STAR alignment and chimeric junction extraction are deterministic, and the guideline asks for record-level matching on the junction coordinate fields while allowing rows and columns in any order. That fits the approximate strategy.

align_plan.reasoning: Both tables use STAR Chimeric.out.junction style records, with the same layout, so no transpose is needed. The seven fields named in the evaluation guideline (chr1, base1, strand1, chr2, base2, strand2, junction_type) have identical names in both tables, so they map directly. They also form the composite row key: they define a junction and are taken straight from STAR's output, not estimated. The reference read_name column holds small integers (0, 6, 7), which look like counts or placeholder values. The candidate read_name holds actual Illumina read IDs. Because the values don't match and the guideline doesn't evaluate this column, it is left unmapped (null). The candidate's 19 extra columns (CIGARs, scores, gene annotations, is_candidate, etc.) are ignored. Row order doesn't matter, so rows are matched by the key and checked as a permutation, with a sort on the key columns to make alignment deterministic. One caveat: the candidate has 757 rows against 434 in the reference. It may include junctions not marked as candidates or repeated junction keys, so some key combinations may appear more than once.

column_configs.name: read_name
column_configs.reasoning: Reference values are float flags (1.0 or NaN), while candidate values are actual read ID strings, so the contents don't correspond. The guideline only requires the junction coordinate, strand and type columns to match, so this column is not evaluated.

comparison_plan.overall_reasoning: The evaluation guideline says a fusion record matches when chr1, base1, strand1, chr2, base2, strand2 and junction_type agree. Those are the ID columns, and alignment already checks them. The only other column the two files share is read_name, and it holds different things in each. In the reference it is a float64 column of 1.0 or NaN, which looks like a flag or an artifact of parsing. In the candidate it holds real sequencing read identifier strings. A cell-by-cell comparison of these two would be meaningless, and the task does not require read_name to match, so I am skipping it. The candidate's extra columns (gene annotations, CIGAR strings, scores and so on) are not in the reference, so they are not compared. As a result, the score comes from how well the ID-column records match.

notes: Scored by overlap of row keys (F1)
